title: Crunchiness of Osmotically Dehydrated Freeze-Dried Strawberries
content: The osmotically dehydrated strawberries in solutions such as sucrose or natural fruit concentrates before drying can significantly affect the texture and nutrient content, which is often insufficient in the diet. In order to achieve the stability of the osmotically dehydrated plant material, further drying is required. The objective of this study was to analyze the effect of osmotic solution type and time of the osmotically dehydration process applied prior to freeze-drying of strawberries on the acoustic, mechanical, and bioactive properties of the dried fruit. Whole “Honeoya” variety strawberries were osmotically dehydrated in a 60 °Brix sucrose and chokeberry juice concentrate solution for 1, 2, and 3 hours at 30°C. After osmotic treatment, the fruit was freeze-dried. The control sample consisted of no osmo-dehydrated freeze-dried strawberries. The texture was assessed using instrumental meth-ods; the acoustic emission (AE) and mechanical properties were measured using the contact method during the compression test. The content of bioactive substances and water activity, and density of freeze-dried fruit were also assessed. Dried fruit after osmotic pretreatment in chokeberry juice con-centrate was characterized by lower final water activity in comparison to the fruit non-dehydrated, and osmotic dehydration in a sucrose solution. The density was also significantly different. The os-motically dehydration of strawberries in a sucrose solution preceding the freeze-drying process re-sulted in increasing the energy of acoustic event and the number of events AE, and force and work did not change significantly in the fruit in comparison with control samples. The osmotic dehydra-tion in chokeberry juice concentrate, on the other hand, had the opposite effect. After 2 and 3 hours, acoustic parameter values decreased, while mechanical parameters increased significantly. Straw-berries dehydrated in sucrose for 2 and 3 hours were characterized by the highest crunchiness, with a crunchiness index of 72 and 38, respectively. Significantly lower crunchiness index was observed for non-dehydrated fruit (10) and for those dehydrated in chokeberry juice concentrate (from 3 to 7). Strawberries, both non-dehydrated and osmotically dehydrated in chokeberry juice concentrate, generated sounds at frequencies between 0.5 and 10 kHz, regardless of the osmotic treatment time before freeze-drying. However, fruits osmotically dehydrated in sucrose solution generated sounds across the entire frequency range (0.5-15 kHz). Strawberries dehydrated for 1 hour and 3 hours in chokeberry juice concentrate contained polyphenols at 4662 and 5001 [mg acid GAE/100 g d.m.]. Lower polyphenols content were found in strawberries dehydrated in sucrose for 1 hour - 2581 [mg acid GAE/100 g d.m.] and 3 hours - 3076 [mg acid GAE/100 g d.m.]. The content of anthocyanins was higher in strawberries osmotically dehydrated in sucrose than in chokeberry juice concentrate. The longer time of the osmo-dehydration process caused an increase in anthocyanins content. Con-sidering the texture, osmotic dehydration in a sucrose solution before freeze-drying strawberries is advantageous due to high crunchiness, as well as increasing the oxidative capacity.
